clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal recessive progeroid disorder combining skeletal dysplasia with partial or generalised lipodystrophy
Type A (MADA) arises from LMNA (lamin A/C) mutations, while type B (MADB) results from ZMPSTE24 mutations affecting prelamin A processing
Skeletal hallmarks include mandibular and clavicular hypoplasia, acro-osteolysis (resorption of the terminal finger phalanges), delayed cranial suture closure, and joint contractures
The MADA fat pattern is typically partial with limb fat loss and relative truncal sparing, whereas MADB tends toward more generalised fat loss with earlier, more severe features
Progeroid skin and features, mottled pigmentation, alopecia, and a beaked nose accompany the phenotype
Loss of subcutaneous fat produces insulin resistance, acanthosis nigricans, and a predisposition to hypertriglyceridaemia and diabetes
Management targets the metabolic complications with insulin sensitisers and lipid control, with leptin (metreleptin) replacement considered when leptin is low
Diagnosis integrates the skeletal-progeroid-lipodystrophy triad with LMNA and ZMPSTE24 genetics
reference.pathophysiology: Mandibuloacral dysplasia is a laminopathy-spectrum disorder caused by biallelic mutations in LMNA, which encodes the nuclear-lamina proteins lamin A/C, or in ZMPSTE24, the metalloprotease that cleaves prelamin A to mature lamin A. Defective lamin processing destabilises the nuclear envelope, impairing the function and survival of mesenchymal-derived tissues including bone and adipocytes. This produces the characteristic mandibular and acral skeletal defects, progeroid connective-tissue changes, and loss of subcutaneous fat. As with other lipodystrophies, reduced fat-storage capacity drives ectopic lipid deposition, insulin resistance, acanthosis nigricans, and a tendency to hypertriglyceridaemia and diabetes.
additionalDifferentials: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria and other progeroid syndromes
Werner syndrome and adult progeroid disorders
Other skeletal dysplasias with metabolic features
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey demonstrating mandibular/clavicular hypoplasia and acro-osteolysis
Regional fat imaging (DEXA/MRI) to characterise the lipodystrophy pattern
Fasting glucose/HbA1c, insulin, and lipid profile
Serum leptin to guide consideration of leptin replacement
Genetic testing of LMNA and ZMPSTE24
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging for steatosis
redFlags: Progressive skeletal deformity and joint contractures limiting function
Rapidly advancing progeroid features in the more severe MADB form
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies with subtype and severity; the LMNA-related type A tends to be milder with a partial lipodystrophy phenotype, whereas the ZMPSTE24-related type B is more severe and progeroid, and long-term outlook is shaped by metabolic and skeletal complications.
pitfalls: Mistaking the disorder for isolated familial partial lipodystrophy and missing the skeletal features
Failing to distinguish the milder LMNA type from the more severe ZMPSTE24 type
Neglecting metabolic screening for diabetes and hypertriglyceridaemia
Not arranging genetic confirmation and counselling
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on lipodystrophy
management: Manage insulin resistance and diabetes with lifestyle measures and insulin-sensitising therapy such as metformin, adding insulin where needed
Treat hypertriglyceridaemia with a low-fat diet plus fibrates and/or statins to reduce pancreatitis and cardiovascular risk
Consider recombinant leptin (metreleptin) replacement in significant lipodystrophy with metabolic complications and low leptin
Undertake metabolic surveillance with fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid profile and monitoring for hepatic steatosis
Provide orthopaedic and physiotherapy input for joint contractures and monitor acro-osteolysis and skeletal dysplasia
Coordinate care across endocrinology, clinical genetics and orthopaedics
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive LMNA or ZMPSTE24 disease with testing of at-risk relatives
